- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., 1.00) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., -1.00), model often underestimates drops; adjust downward by 5–10% of recent trend or add a buffer for volatility.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day post-spike.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., after 70–75 range, price drops to 65–68), model often fails to recognize it; apply a “reversion bias” rule: if 3 consecutive days above 75, reduce forecast by 1–2% daily.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to be overly optimistic in early days (e.g., first 5–7 days); apply a “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 0.5–1% per day for first 7 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment history shows alternating +/– spikes (e.g., +1, -1, +1), model often misreads momentum; use a “sentiment filter”: if sentiment alternates, reduce forecast volatility by 20–30%.
- When true outcome shows a sharp drop after a spike (e.g., 75 → 65), model often fails to anticipate; add a “drop buffer” rule: if spike > 10%, reduce forecast by 5–8% for next 3 days.
